reference.source: Moss and Adams' Heart Disease in Infants, Children and Adolescents
clinicalPearls: The left pulmonary artery arises anomalously from the right pulmonary artery and courses between the trachea and oesophagus to reach the left lung, forming a sling around the distal trachea and right main bronchus.
It is the only vascular anomaly that passes between the trachea and oesophagus, giving a unique anterior indentation on the oesophagus at barium swallow.
It frequently coexists with complete (O-shaped) tracheal cartilage rings and long-segment congenital tracheal stenosis, the so-called ring-sling complex.
Infants typically present early with stridor, wheeze, recurrent respiratory infection and respiratory distress from airway compression.
Because associated tracheal stenosis often dominates the clinical picture, airway assessment is as important as defining the vascular anatomy.
CT or MR angiography demonstrates the aberrant vessel, and bronchoscopy is essential to evaluate the trachea for complete rings and the level and length of stenosis.
Surgical treatment involves division and re-implantation of the left pulmonary artery onto the main pulmonary artery, typically on cardiopulmonary bypass.
Coexisting significant tracheal stenosis is addressed concurrently, commonly by slide tracheoplasty.
reference.pathophysiology: The left pulmonary artery normally develops from the left sixth aortic arch; in a pulmonary artery sling it fails to form from this precursor and instead arises from the right pulmonary artery, so that to reach the left hilum it must pass over the right main bronchus and course posteriorly between the trachea and oesophagus. This aberrant vessel forms a partial sling that compresses the distal trachea and right main bronchus anteriorly and, lying behind the trachea, indents the oesophagus anteriorly. The developmental disturbance is frequently accompanied by intrinsic tracheal maldevelopment with complete cartilage rings and diffuse narrowing, compounding the extrinsic compression and producing severe fixed airway obstruction.
additionalDifferentials: Complete vascular rings such as double aortic arch or right arch with aberrant subclavian
Congenital tracheal stenosis without a sling
additionalInvestigations: Transthoracic echocardiography to delineate the anomalous origin and associated cardiac lesions
Flexible and rigid bronchoscopy to assess complete rings and stenosis
Contrast oesophagogram showing an anterior oesophageal indentation
Chest radiograph noting asymmetric aeration, a low right hilum and air trapping
Ventilation-perfusion or pulmonary function assessment in older children
redFlags: Severe stridor with respiratory distress or apnoeic episodes in infancy
Recurrent or lobar pneumonia with persistent air trapping
Difficult intubation or inability to pass beyond a narrowed trachea
reference.prognosis: With modern surgical re-implantation and, where needed, tracheal reconstruction, outcomes have improved substantially, though prognosis is worse with extensive long-segment tracheal stenosis or associated cardiac anomalies.
pitfalls: Focusing on the vascular anomaly and failing to assess the trachea for complete rings and stenosis.
Misinterpreting the anterior oesophageal indentation, which is unique to this lesion.
Delayed diagnosis through mislabelling as asthma or recurrent bronchiolitis.
Not planning simultaneous airway reconstruction when significant stenosis is present.
Assuming that vessel re-implantation alone will relieve fixed intrinsic tracheal narrowing.
references: Moss and Adams' Heart Disease in Infants, Children and Adolescents
management: Surgical division and re-implantation of the anomalous left pulmonary artery onto the main pulmonary artery to relieve the tracheobronchial sling
Concurrent tracheal reconstruction such as slide tracheoplasty for associated long-segment stenosis with complete cartilage rings
Airway stabilisation and respiratory support for the compromised infant before definitive repair
Bronchoscopic assessment of the trachea for complete rings and the level and length of stenosis to plan intervention
Echocardiography and cross-sectional angiography to define the vascular anatomy and detect associated cardiac lesions
Postoperative airway surveillance for residual stenosis, granulation or restenosis, with bronchoscopic intervention as needed
Multidisciplinary cardiothoracic, airway and paediatric intensive care management
